name: Baseline analyst
notice: Simulation based on public material; not the person's own words.

D01.one_line: Frontier pre-training is locked up by industry compute (industry accounts for over 90% of notable models); academia's marginal contribution lies in methodology/data analysis, not in scale itself.
D01.late_modes: Piling on parameter scale is already locked up by industry compute and hard for an individual to enter.

D02.one_line: Whether RLVR merely reweights the existing sampling distribution rather than teaching new capability is still an open question, and academia can run clean experiments with small models.
D02.late_modes: Pure engineering work that replicates vendors' RLHF pipelines and tunes parameters already has very low marginal returns.

D03.one_line: Treat continual learning/credit assignment and RSI separately: the former is a solid academic problem, while the existing evidence on the latter all points to it being far off.
D03.late_modes: Conceptual self-improving agent demos are already too late; without rigorous ablation they struggle to get attention.

D04.one_line: The scaffolding layer is being absorbed by the models themselves (the top 9 on Terminal-Bench are all vendors' general CLI agents), and the space for academia-specific contributions is narrowing.
D04.late_modes: Designing a new agent harness/scaffolding is already too late; it is being absorbed by the models themselves.

D05.one_line: Evaluation does not directly produce capability, but it decides the credibility of other directions; statistical rigor and the trust boundary of judges are among academia's few real advantages (Arena itself began in academia).
D05.late_modes: Building yet another static leaderboard is already too late; it is easy to game and hard to keep credible.

D06.one_line: The gap in touch/force data and failures of cross-embodiment transfer are real unsolved problems, and low-cost hardware (SO-101 and others) has pushed the bar for academic experiments low enough.
D06.late_modes: Fine-tuning an off-the-shelf VLA for a new-task demo is already too late; research on reliability/generalization mechanisms is still open.

D07.one_line: Action representation (diffusion head vs autoregressive/parallel decoding) has solid empirical comparisons (OpenVLA-OFT, FAST) and does not depend only on marketing coinages (WAM).
D07.late_modes: Repackaging existing methods under the new WAM label is already too late and has no real novelty.

D08.one_line: The biggest paradigm bet, but 'video generation = world model' itself has not been proven (it fails on out-of-distribution physics); frontier work is quickly being pulled away by private capital/startups.
D08.late_modes: Simply building more realistic video-generation demos is already too late; too many teams are doing it.

D09.one_line: Simulation is one of the few scalable ways for robot learning to escape the cost of collecting real data, and SIMPLER shows that academia can make real methodological impact.
D09.late_modes: Building a new simulator platform has declining added value; there are already many platforms.

D10.one_line: The real levers (fleet long-tail data, safety validation) are monopolized by a few companies, and the success rate on the simulation benchmark academia can reach (CARLA 2.0) is only about 6%.
D10.late_modes: Paper-style end-to-end planning work without fleet data already has very low marginal value.

D11.one_line: BLINK/VSI-Bench show the spatial-reasoning gap is still huge, and diagnostic benchmarks are themselves the contribution form academia is best at and that is adopted most.
D11.late_modes: The edge in training yet another VLM to chase existing leaderboards is already thin.

D12.one_line: Unified understanding-and-generation models are generally worse than specialized ones (RealUnify, UniG2U-Bench), and diagnosing interference mechanisms has more academic leverage than building another unified model.
D12.late_modes: Simply chasing image/video generation quality leaderboards is already too late; top vendors dominate.

D13.one_line: Interpretability methodology is still in heavy flux (DeepMind itself lowered the priority of SAEs) and suits rigorous comparison by academia.
D13.late_modes: Building yet another SAE variant is a route whose evidence is already relatively weak.

D14.one_line: FlashAttention shows that academia can build systems-algorithm co-design components that are really adopted, but it requires a strong systems background.

D15.one_line: AlphaEvolve shows the value is real, but in most applications (such as single-cell perturbation prediction) deep models have not consistently beaten simple baselines.

D16.one_line: Generative methods have indeed been deployed in industrial recommendation (Tencent TGR), but the compute cost is high (Meituan case: 10-100x).

lever_reason: The hard constraints of physical AI are real data and transferable simulation, not the algorithms themselves; evaluation is a quality-inspection layer, not a production function; world models have great potential but have not been validated in a closed loop, so they get medium-high weight, not the highest.

Q2.condition: Narrow-domain model + compute at scale (such as 64 H100s for months) + a team of 2-4 + open weights that can be adopted externally; otherwise it is better to dig deep into a specific subproblem.

cruxes.question: Is evaluation science the most reliable lever for the next 5-10 years, or merely quality inspection for other levers rather than a driving force?
cruxes.my_position: Evaluation is a necessary condition for trust, not a production function of capability; real data + simulation + RL are the direct driving forces, and evaluation decides whether their output can be believed.
cruxes.would_change_if: If there is evidence that a better evaluation method directly led to a model's capability improvement, rather than only helping us choose models better, I would raise the weight.

cruxes.question: Are the representations learned by video/JEPA-type predictive models already really usable by policies, or can they merely be read out but not used?
cruxes.my_position: Existing evidence (V-JEPA2-AC's planning horizon is only 1 step; POKEWORLD separates read-out from use) says it is not yet usable, and closed-loop causal evidence is needed.
cruxes.would_change_if: If there were long-horizon closed-loop control work on real robots with strict ablation showing that the policy truly depends on the representation rather than a shortcut, I would consider it solved.

cruxes.question: Training a narrow-domain foundation model at academic compute scale (such as a hundred-card H100 cluster): a real opportunity, or a structural lag, destined to be matched by industry?
cruxes.my_position: When narrow domain + open weights + a path to outside adoption are all present, it is a real opportunity (precedents: Olmo3, FlashAttention, DPO); without all three it is just amusing oneself.
cruxes.would_change_if: If, over the next two years, cases of outside adoption of narrow-domain academic models (VLA/world models) keep growing rather than being quickly replaced by industry versions, I would be more sure it is a real opportunity.

taste_advice: First work one concrete, causally verifiable small problem deeply and thoroughly; do not rush to chase the label of a big narrative (world models/agents/scaling) itself.

pairwise.why: If world models hold up, they are the bigger paradigm bet; evaluation is a necessary quality-inspection layer and does not directly produce new capability.
Embodied AI has clearer, verifiable real bottlenecks, and evaluation remains a supporting role.
D06's bottleneck is more concrete and verifiable (touch/cross-embodiment transfer failures), while the core assumption of D08 is still disputed on validity.
D07 already has solid real-robot comparison data (OpenVLA-OFT and others), while the core assumption of D08 is still disputed.
Simulation is a key method, but core difficulties such as reliability/touch/generalization cannot be solved by simulation alone.
RLVR already has a solid evidence chain for capability improvement; the current evidence on RSI/continual learning shows limited effect.
The generative direction has open problems (few-step generation, unified modeling) that are more valuable now.
Frontier pre-training scale is locked up by industry compute, while in evaluation methodology academia still has a scarce advantage that can be adopted.
The scaffolding layer is being absorbed by models and its leverage is falling; continual learning/credit assignment is still an open scientific problem.
Evaluation-methodology problems are more concrete and testable; interpretability tools themselves are still in heavy flux with no settled conclusion.
The real levers of autonomous driving (fleet data/safety validation) are monopolized by a few companies; embodied AI has more real problems within reach.
